items.title: Module - 7 - Courage, ReconciliACTION, and My Role as an Educator
items.summary: 1. Role Models and Mentors In his TEDx talk, Brad Baker emphasizes that "it will take courage for us to be successful in…
items.content_html:
1. Role Models and Mentors
In his TEDx talk, Brad Baker emphasizes that "it will take courage for us to be successful in education" and to change the system. This really made me think about my own journey:

- My Role Models: My greatest role models are those educators who prove that every child can succeed when they feel valued and supported. I truly believe that meaningful learning only happens when we build strong, caring relationships with students and their families.

- My Mentors: As I work to integrate Indigenous perspectives, my essential mentors are local Elders, Knowledge Keepers, and Indigenous educators. Listening to their voices is the only way to teach with real authenticity and respect.

2. Living ReconciliACTION
Roberta Jamieson notes that “Reconciliation is not just a noun... it is also a verb.” She calls this ReconciliACTION, which resonates deeply with my vision as a teacher:

What it means to me: It means reconciliation isn't a one-time event or a textbook chapter; it is a daily practice. It means acknowledging the truth of Canada's past and making intentional choices every day to create equity and belonging in my classroom.

Fostering Allyship: I can share this mindset with my students by encouraging empathy, curiosity, and critical thinking. By bringing Indigenous stories and local community connections into the classroom, I want to teach youth that being an ally is an active commitment.

3. Walking the Path in My District
Investigating the work in the Mission Public School District (SD75) gives me a lot of hope. The district is actively walking the path toward an inclusive, antiracist system by:

Recognizing and honoring local Stó:lō territories.

Collaborating genuinely with local Indigenous communities.

Implementing the First Peoples Principles of Learning to ensure education is holistic and relational.

Key Takeaway
Ultimately, this reflection reminds me that building a just school system is an ongoing journey. I choose to embrace the courage Brad Baker speaks of to keep challenging my own assumptions, and the commitment to live reconciliation as the active verb Roberta Jamieson described.

items.title: Module - 7- What is reconciliation?
items.summary: Before moving to Canada, the word "reconciliation" felt like an abstract concept to me, something I associated broadly with international human rights and…
items.content_html:
Before moving to Canada, the word "reconciliation" felt like an abstract concept to me, something I associated broadly with international human rights and social justice. However, stepping into the Canadian context, and specifically into the world of education, completely shifted my perspective. I quickly realized that here, reconciliation is not a theoretical idea; it is a profound, deeply personal, and ongoing necessity tied to the lived experiences of Indigenous Peoples, the painful history of residential schools, and the lingering echoes of colonialism.

As I have listened, studied, and grown in my role, I’ve come to understand that reconciliation doesn’t carry a single, uniform definition. It means different things to different stakeholders. For some, the heart of reconciliation lies in truth-telling, uncovering and acknowledging the unvarnished, painful history of the past. For others, it is about action: rebuilding broken relationships, fiercely respecting Indigenous rights, and ensuring self-determination and equity for communities. Witnessing these diverse perspectives has taught me that reconciliation isn’t a final destination or a box to check; it is a continuous, lifelong journey of learning and unlearning.

To figure out where I fit into this process, I have tried to intentionally lean into the discomfort of learning a history that wasn't originally my own. I have engaged with course readings, participated in professional development, and, most importantly, listened to Indigenous voices. As an educator, I constantly reflect on the immense responsibility we hold. The classroom can either perpetuate old harms or become a space of healing, and I want to ensure my practice always leans toward the latter by creating spaces rooted in genuine respect and accurate, honest histories.

Facing ahead, I know my learning is nowhere near finished. I want to continue reading works by Indigenous authors, listening to community elders, and learning from Indigenous educators. My goal is to move beyond just knowing the history to truly understanding and honoring Indigenous ways of knowing and relating. I want to bring these perspectives into my teaching practice not as an afterthought, but respectfully, authentically, and from the heart, doing my small part to shape a truly inclusive and equitable future for the children I teach.

REFERENCES:

Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. (n.d.). What is reconciliation? CBC Kids News.

Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. (n.d.). Learning the unvarnished history of Canada is key to reconciliation with Jody Wilson-Raybould. CBC News.

Healthy Canadians. (n.d.). Reconciliation: What does it mean? Government of Canada.

items.title: Module - 6 - Reflection
items.summary: This module really pushed me to deepen my understanding of Indigenous education and challenge my own assumptions about creating inclusive, culturally responsive classrooms.
items.content_html:
This module really pushed me to deepen my understanding of Indigenous education and challenge my own assumptions about creating inclusive, culturally responsive classrooms. Between the readings, videos, and discussions, I walked away with a much clearer, more nuanced grasp of decolonization, Indigenization, authentic resources, assessment, and cultural safety.

Artifacts and Key Takeaways

  • Decolonization vs. Indigenization Comparison Chart: Creating this chart was a turning point for me. It helped me realize that while both concepts work toward transforming education, they aren't interchangeable. Decolonization is about actively questioning and dismantling colonial structures, whereas Indigenization focuses on weaving Indigenous ways of knowing, learning, and being into our educational spaces. This activity made me look much closer at the language I use and the actual intentions behind my teaching.
  • Summary and Reflection on Potlatch as Pedagogy: This piece highlighted just how vital relationships, reciprocity, storytelling, and community are to the learning process. It was a great reminder that meaningful learning is rooted in experience and connection. As an elementary teacher, I can bring this into my classroom by making more room for collaborative learning, oral storytelling, and genuine community involvement.
  • Annotated Bibliography of Authentic Indigenous Resources: This task drove home the responsibility we have to choose materials created directly by Indigenous authors, organizations, and Knowledge Keepers. I learned that authenticity takes careful vetting—just because a resource claims to represent an Indigenous perspective doesn't mean it’s accurate or respectful. Moving forward, this will guide how I curate classroom materials to ensure Indigenous voices are represented properly.
  • Assessment Tool Designed Using Indigenous Frameworks: This was easily one of the most practical assignments in the module because it forced me to rethink assessment beyond traditional academic metrics. I explored ways to center student voice, self-reflection, relationships, and holistic growth. Going forward, I want to keep designing assessments that value different ways of showing learning and celebrate the unique strengths of every student.
  • Reflection on Cultural Safety: The resources and discussions surrounding this topic made me hyper-aware of how deeply systemic, ongoing colonial practices still impact Indigenous students and their families today. I spent a lot of time reflecting on actionable strategies: building trust, weaving Indigenous perspectives naturally throughout the entire school year, and fostering a classroom environment where everyone feels safe and actually belongs. These are practices I am committed to strengthening.

Conclusion and Inquiry Connection

This module ties directly into my inquiry project by providing concrete, practical strategies to build a learning environment that genuinely respects and responds to Indigenous perspectives. It has also reinforced the idea that this work requires continuous learning and self-reflection.

Blending my past teaching experience with everything I’ve learned over these first six modules, I feel incredibly well-equipped to integrate Indigenous perspectives meaningfully—not as isolated, check-the-box activities, but as an organic part of my practice. My ultimate goal is to keep building authentic relationships, sourcing proper materials, and creating learning experiences that honor Indigenous knowledge while supporting every single learner in my room

items.title: Module - 6 - Building Relationships in SD75       (Mission, BC)
items.summary: Building Relationships in SD75 Inviting an Elder or Knowledge Keeper to our classroom isn't just a "check-a-box" activity on the curriculum; it's opening…
items.content_html:
Building Relationships in SD75
Inviting an Elder or Knowledge Keeper to our classroom isn't just a "check-a-box" activity on the curriculum; it's opening the door to a living relationship. After reviewing this week's readings and analyzing the reality of our district (SD75, Mission), I'm left with several key reflections:

Real vs. Theoretical Accessibility: While the Siwal Si'wes department does incredible work and has guidelines available, just having a PDF stored online isn't enough. We need these protocols to be lived and actively shared during Professional Development Days (Pro-D Days), ensuring that both new and substitute teachers know how to approach them respectfully.

Humanizing the Protocol: It's vital that the district's administrative processes adapt to the warmth of the cultural protocol. This involves ensuring that compensation and recognition for the Elders' time are handled efficiently and promptly, and that the document details the local specificities of the Stó:lō people, such as the proper use of ceremonial tobacco and the logistics to ensure their comfort and well-being during the visit.

Beyond the Classroom: As an educator, I know I'm not alone in this. We have important allies: from the Mission Friendship Centre to connect with the urban Indigenous community, to the education offices of local bands like Leq'á:mel. Furthermore, collaborating with local land and salmon stewards in Mission allows us to co-design land-based learning that truly honors traditional environmental stewardship.

Ultimately, protocol is not a rule to be followed, but rather the foundation for building genuine relationships based on respect, reciprocity, and cultural humility.

References 
Alberta Teachers’ Association. (2021). Elder protocol. https://www.teachers.ab.ca/

First Peoples Cultural Council. (2021). Working with Elders. https://fpcc.ca/

Indigenous Corporate Training Inc. (2017). 7 tips on building relationships with Indigenous Peoples. https://www.ictinc.ca/

National Association of Friendship Centres. (2023). National Association of Friendship Centres. https://nafc.ca/

items.title: Module - 5 - Reflection
items.summary: In this module, I selected five artifacts that represent my learning journey and the development of my understanding of Indigenous perspectives, reconciliation, and…
items.content_html:
In this module, I selected five artifacts that represent my learning journey and the development of my understanding of Indigenous perspectives, reconciliation, and decolonization in education. Through these, I seek to connect this knowledge with my future teaching practice in Canada.

Cultural Safety: Historical trauma (colonialism, residential schools) continues to affect the present. To incorporate this into my educational practice, it is necessary to create inclusive, safe, and respectful learning spaces that also involve families and the community.

Leadership and Role Models: Sports (e.g., Ethan Bear) serve as a platform for cultural pride and advocacy. This demonstrates the importance of highlighting Indigenous role models so that students value their contributions to society.

Linguistic Revitalization: Language is directly related to identity and culture. In my teaching practice, I aspire to support the integration of Indigenous languages in British Columbia schools by incorporating words, place names, and local perspectives into the classroom.

Digital Self-Representation: Social media allows Indigenous youth to tell their own stories. As an educator, I want to create spaces for my students to critically evaluate media and appreciate diverse voices and perspectives.

Decolonization and Resurgence: It is wonderful to learn about Indigenous self-determination and community leadership. I felt this as a call to transform my practices to value Indigenous knowledge systems and promote respectful relationships.

My General Reflection and Future Practice
Throughout these five modules, I have developed a much deeper understanding of Indigenous histories, cultures, and contemporary realities in Canada. Although I already had some knowledge from my work in schools, this course is helping me to become more aware and directly connect it to broader concepts such as reconciliation and decolonization.

For my inquiry project and my daily work in the classroom, I feel it as a call to commit to creating environments that promote inclusion, respect for Indigenous ways of knowing, and building strong relationships with families and communities.

items.title: Module - 5- Revitalization of Indigenous Languages
items.summary: Language plays a vital role in cultural identity and well-being. Through language, people connect with their history, traditions, values, and community. As a…
items.content_html:
Language plays a vital role in cultural identity and well-being. Through language, people connect with their history, traditions, values, and community. As a Spanish speaker, my language helps me maintain a connection to my cultural roots and allows me to express my thoughts, emotions, and experiences. When my daughter relies solely on English, I try to encourage her by speaking only to her in Spanish so she doesn't lose her identity. Language is much more than a communication tool; it's an important part of who we are.

Reflecting on the revitalization of Indigenous languages, I realize I haven't observed much of it in my immediate neighborhood because I don't usually interact closely with my neighbors due to time constraints. Therefore, I'm not fully aware of the extent to which Indigenous languages ​​are being used or revitalized in my local community.

However, through my work in schools as an educational assistant and my everyday life, I have noticed several significant efforts to honor and promote Indigenous languages ​​and cultures. In some schools, Indigenous words and phrases are displayed on hallway bulletin boards and classroom materials. One practice I find particularly meaningful takes place at a traditional elementary school where, each morning after singing the national anthem, a second-grade class acknowledges the traditional territory in which the school is located using an Indigenous language. Outside of school, I have also noticed that on some major highways, the road signs include Indigenous place names alongside English ones. These daily practices and visual reminders help everyone develop awareness and respect for Indigenous peoples and their connection to the land.

I am also familiar with C̓əsqənelə Elementary School in Maple Ridge. The fact that the school bears an Indigenous name demonstrates a commitment to recognizing and honoring Indigenous language and culture within the education system. Actions like these help make Indigenous languages ​​more visible and valued in everyday life.

I believe more can be done to support the revitalization of Indigenous languages. Schools could increase opportunities for students to learn Indigenous greetings, songs, stories, and place names. Communities could support language classes, cultural events, and partnerships with Indigenous elders and keepers of knowledge. Technology, books, films, and digital resources can also play an important role in making Indigenous languages ​​accessible to younger generations.

Seeing all these efforts also touches me personally—it strengthens my own desire to keep my culture alive. I feel that I was the one who chose to come to Canada, and instead of others adapting to my culture, I can learn and embrace the Indigenous culture of this land without abandoning my roots. Every time I do something related to my culture, I feel like I have a little piece of Colombia with me.

Language protection and education must be prioritized because language carries cultural knowledge, traditions, and ways of understanding the world. Losing a language means losing a piece of human history, while keeping it alive brings deep healing, pride, and emotional well-being to the communities. Supporting Indigenous languages ​​contributes to reconciliation, strengthens cultural identity, and helps ensure that future generations can continue learning about and celebrating Indigenous cultures. Preserving these languages ​​is not only important for Indigenous communities but also for Canadian society as a whole.

items.title: Module - 5 - Indigeneity and Technology
items.summary: Do you think social media allows for positive self-representation among young people? I believe that, depending on the context, social media can allow…
items.content_html:
Do you think social media allows for positive self-representation among young people?

I believe that, depending on the context, social media can allow for positive self-representation among young people, as long as it is used thoughtfully and responsibly. Platforms such as Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, and Snapchat can foster connection by allowing young people to share their experiences, cultures, personal talents, and perspectives.  The video featuring Marika Sila and Kairyn Potts clearly demonstrates how Indigenous youth use social media to celebrate their identities and challenge stereotypes. Likewise, social media can help young people connect with communities and build support networks, encouraging them to reflect on and take pride in their backgrounds and experiences.  

2. What other lingering questions might you have about self-representation and challenging stereotypes and assumptions?

One question I still have is how educators can guide students in developing a critical perspective on the content they encounter on social media while also encouraging them to use it as a tool for self-expression and positive self-representation.  I am also interested in exploring how schools and social media platforms can actively support the sharing of authentic information, thereby reducing misinformation and harmful stereotypes.  Finally, I would like to better understand how digital technologies can be optimally leveraged to ensure that Indigenous voices are heard, valued, and represented fairly and respectfully. Specifically, how can we as educators use intentional digital curation to build a seamless, respectful bridge between land-based learning and contemporary educational environments?

items.title: Modules - 3 & 4 - Reflection
items.summary: Artifacts What I learned Connecting with My Teaching Practice and Inquiry Project Reflection on Biases and Teaching This activity led me to reflect…
items.content_html:
Artifacts What I learned Connecting with My Teaching Practice and Inquiry Project
Reflection on Biases and Teaching This activity led me to reflect on how personal experiences and systemic biases influence our worldviews. Acknowledging that these behavioral tendencies exist within all of us—and addressing them from a place of shared humanity—is a significant step toward ensuring they do not impact our pedagogical decisions or the relationships we build with our students. Critically examining my own beliefs to dismantle personal biases is vital to ensuring that every student feels valued. This insight aligns seamlessly with my professional commitment to fostering inclusive and equitable educational environments.
Doctrine of Discovery Reflection I learned about the historical impact of the Doctrine of Discovery and understood how its effects continue to influence the relationship between Indigenous peoples and government institutions today. This reminded me of how important it is to teach history by looking at different perspectives and listening to the voices of the people who actually experienced it. Doing this helps students develop critical thinking. It also strengthened my commitment to helping with reconciliation and healing through education.
Learning From the Land Reflection When we connect learning with the land and nature, we offer more meaningful experiences that stay in the minds and hearts of our students. This helps them build a deep relationship with the world around them. This reflection inspired me to look for more learning opportunities outside the classroom and to bring in hands-on activities that connect school subjects with the real world. This is also directly related to my interest in bringing Indigenous perspectives into science education.
Indigenous Narratives and Colonization Reflection

I looked at how the main stories we are told have shaped our understanding of history, and how other voices have often been left out. I realized how important it is to listen to and value different kinds of knowledge. This reminded me that every story has more than one side, and we should always listen to both perspectives.

 As a teacher, I want to create spaces where different perspectives are recognized and respected. This learning helps my inquiry project by giving me a better understanding of how to include Indigenous ways of knowing in real and meaningful ways.

Final Reflection

These modules helped me see even more clearly that education plays a vital role in building respectful relationships and helping with reconciliation. I learned that teaching is not just about passing down information, but about making knowledge meaningful. This made me reflect on my responsibility as a teacher to notice my own biases and question the main historical stories we are told. Since history is usually written by people in power, we need to create opportunities for students to learn from different points of view.

Regarding my inquiry project, these experiences have strengthened my interest in finding ways to include Indigenous perspectives in my teaching. I truly believe that learning from the land and nature, valuing different kinds of knowledge, and thinking critically about history are key to creating a more inclusive and meaningful education for all students.

items.title: Module - 4 - Learning Through Circles: Listening, Respect, and Community.
items.summary: These readings helped me associate circles with spaces that have clear intentions, promoting respect and active listening, as well as reflection and the…
items.content_html:
These readings helped me associate circles with spaces that have clear intentions, promoting respect and active listening, as well as reflection and the building of meaningful relationships. This last aspect is particularly beautiful; circles are not just spaces for sharing opinions. In a circle, we have the opportunity to look at each other, understand our expressions, and see beyond the words.

Circles create opportunities for each participant to be heard without rigid hierarchical levels, thus fostering more equitable participation. This is what makes the difference compared to other forms of communication, such as debates where the goal is always for one side to be right, or lectures where the objective is usually the unilateral transmission of knowledge.

As an educator, I've enjoyed working with circles before, though, to be honest, not fromthis specific restorative perspective. Drawing from my experience with Montessori pedagogy, I have always considered circles a valuable tool for welcoming activities, group reflections, conflict resolution, and creating spaces where students can respectfully express their emotions, thus developing empathy and a deep sense of belonging.
One of the most important takeaways from these readings is that dialogue circles have deep roots in Indigenous traditions. For this reason, it's crucial to understand Indigenous protocols before implementing a sharing circle. Without this knowledge, there's a risk of using the practice superficially or out of context. Truly understanding its origin and meaning demonstrates respect for Indigenous communities and helps prevent cultural appropriation.

Overall, this learning made me reflect on the importance of creating spaces where students not only learn academic content but also how to listen to and respect one another, building positive and lasting relationships.

items.title: Module - 4 - Child and Identity Protection
items.summary: It has been difficult for me to grasp why Indigenous children are still overrepresented in the child welfare system across Canada. These resources…
items.content_html:
It has been difficult for me to grasp why Indigenous children are still overrepresented in the child welfare system across Canada. These resources helped me realize how the systems of colonization continue to affect Indigenous families today through separation, inequality, and the loss of cultural connection. In other words, it's not just something from the past—sadly, it keeps happening.


Learning about Jordan’s Principle was moving because it clearly shows how government systems negatively impact children's lives. Children deserve equal access to healthcare, education, and support, without discrimination or delays. It has been a long road that at first seemed to have no end in sight, but fortunately, it is finally taking shape.

I was also really interested in learning about traditional Inuit adoption, as I had zero knowledge of this practice before this module. Now I see that it is deeply connected to Inuit culture, kinship, and community care. The well-being of children guarantees a balanced society when we actually respect their culture, rather than forcing colonial policies and guidelines on them.

Cindy Blackstock helped me better understand the importance of equity in education and child welfare. Equity is not the same as equality; we have to look at the inequalities within the system and provide children with exactly what they need based on their individual circumstances. Every child deserves to grow up in an environment where they feel safe, respected, valued, and connected to their identity and culture.


How can the educational system and preservice teacher training regarding the prioritizing of safety for Indigenous children be improved?

This course has significantly shifted how I think and feel about these issues. Honestly, I'm not entirely sure how long this type of training has been a requirement in teacher education programs. But like I’ve felt since the beginning of this module, this shouldn't be an isolated topic we check off a list just to comply with government policies. It needs to be implemented with genuine feeling. School districts should continue to promote this in Pro-D days and other training spaces, while reminding us that it's okay to ask for help or consult an expert when we're unsure of what to say.

Schools must work alongside families, communities, and Indigenous Elders to create safer, more inclusive environments. Educators need ongoing training that helps them recognize their own biases, address Indigenous topics with respect, and support children with true empathy and cultural understanding.

This just reinforces my belief that education shouldn't be solely about academic learning. We have a responsibility to protect children and create safe spaces, not just for intellectual growth, but for their feelings and emotions. When we feel valued, our minds and bodies simply work better.
